## Market Overview

A quick look at the apparel and fashion analytics market captured in our filtered data. After applying the NAICS 458 filter and checking a list of known apparel and fashion employers, we ended up with 19 verified job postings.

Since the sample is intentionally narrow, the results are best used to understand this specific set of postings. They should not be treated as a representation of the overall analytics job market.

```{python}
#| output: false

import os
import brand
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from matplotlib.ticker import MaxNLocator
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

# Final cleaned dataset
clean_df = pd.read_csv(
    "data/processed/apparel_analyst_clean.csv"
)

print("Dataset shape:", clean_df.shape)

print("\nKey EDA summary:")

print("Total postings:", len(clean_df))
print("Unique job titles:", clean_df["TITLE_CLEAN"].nunique())
print("Unique companies:", clean_df["COMPANY_CLEAN"].nunique())
print("Unique locations:", clean_df["LOCATION"].nunique())

print("\nNon-null salary values:")
print("SALARY_FROM:", clean_df["SALARY_FROM"].notna().sum())
print("SALARY_TO:", clean_df["SALARY_TO"].notna().sum())

print("\nRemote type values:")
print(
    clean_df["REMOTE_TYPE_NAME"]
    .fillna("Missing")
    .value_counts()
)

# Filtered dataset before missing salary and experience values were filled
raw_df = pd.read_csv(
    "data/interim/apparel_analyst_filtered.csv"
)

# Folder for figures used on the website
os.makedirs(
    "figures/market_baseline",
    exist_ok=True
)
```

## Job Volume by Title or Segment

Job titles provide an initial view of the types of analytics roles represented within the selected apparel and fashion market.

```{python}

import plotly.express as px

title_counts = (
    clean_df["TITLE_CLEAN"]
    .dropna()
    .value_counts()
    .head(10)
    .reset_index()
)

title_counts.columns = ["Job Title", "Number of Job Postings"]

fig = px.bar(
    title_counts.sort_values("Number of Job Postings"),
    x="Number of Job Postings",
    y="Job Title",
    orientation="h",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#69558E"],
    title="Top Job Titles in Apparel Analytics"
)

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    yaxis_title="Job Title",
    height=550,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=60, b=20)
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 1: Top Job Titles in Apparel Analytics*

The 19 postings cover a fairly wide mix of roles, including analyst, business intelligence, ecommerce, merchandise, and senior analytics positions. Most titles appear only once, so there is not one dominant job title in the sample. Instead, analytics work seems to be spread across several business functions in apparel and fashion retail.

## Functional Role Segmentation

Individual job titles in the sample are highly fragmented, with many titles appearing only once. To identify broader hiring patterns, the titles are grouped into functional categories based on the primary focus of each role. This provides a more interpretable view of the types of analytics work represented in the selected apparel and fashion job postings.

```{python}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

import plotly.express as px


def classify_role(title):
    title = str(title).lower()

    if any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "business intelligence",
        "data analyst",
        "data governance",
        "data analytics"
    ]):
        return "BI / Data Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "operations",
        "operational",
        "region operations"
    ]):
        return "Operations Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "marketing",
        "media",
        "customer",
        "consumer",
        "digital analytics"
    ]):
        return "Marketing / Customer Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "merchandising",
        "merchandise",
        "ecommerce",
        "e-commerce",
        "retail",
        "wholesale",
        "sales planning"
    ]):
        return "Merchandising / Ecommerce"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "finance",
        "financial",
        "fp&a",
        "strategy",
        "strategic"
    ]):
        return "Finance / Strategy Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "product",
        "engineering"
    ]):
        return "Product / Engineering Analytics"

    else:
        return "Other Analytics"


# Create broader functional role categories
clean_df["ROLE_SEGMENT"] = clean_df["TITLE_CLEAN"].apply(classify_role)

# Count postings within each functional area
role_segment_counts = (
    clean_df["ROLE_SEGMENT"]
    .value_counts()
    .reset_index()
)

role_segment_counts.columns = [
    "Functional Area",
    "Number of Job Postings"
]

# Sort so the horizontal chart reads from smaller to larger values
role_segment_counts = role_segment_counts.sort_values(
    "Number of Job Postings",
    ascending=True
)

# Display counts for validation
# print(role_segment_counts)

# Check whether any titles remain uncategorized
# print("\nTitles classified as Other Analytics:")

other_titles = clean_df.loc[
    clean_df["ROLE_SEGMENT"] == "Other Analytics",
    "TITLE_CLEAN"
]

# if len(other_titles) == 0:
#     print("None")
# else:
#     print(other_titles.to_string(index=False))

# Create interactive Plotly chart
fig_role_segments = px.bar(
    role_segment_counts,
    x="Number of Job Postings",
    y="Functional Area",
    orientation="h",
    template="group7",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#69558E"],
    title="Job Postings by Functional Analytics Area"
)

fig_role_segments.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    height=450,
    xaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    yaxis_title="Functional Area"
)

fig_role_segments.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig_role_segments.show()
```
*Figure 2: Job Postings by Functional Analytics Area*

The functional segmentation shows that BI and data analytics roles represent the largest share of the selected sample, with 6 of the 19 postings. Marketing and customer analytics follows closely with 5 postings, while merchandising and ecommerce account for 3. Finance and strategy analytics and operations analytics each contribute 2 postings, and product or engineering analytics contributes 1.

This broader grouping reveals that analytics hiring within the selected apparel and fashion sample is distributed across several business functions rather than being concentrated in a single type of role. Because the dataset is small and the categories are derived from job-title wording, the results should be interpreted as a descriptive view of the selected postings rather than a standardized representation of the broader industry.

## Data Completeness Across Key Attributes

Several analytical fields in the job-posting dataset contain substantial missing information. Comparing attribute coverage helps distinguish which findings are supported by most of the sample and which rely on a smaller subset of postings.

```{python}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

total_postings = len(raw_df)

# Count only clearly identified work-arrangement values.
# Missing and "Unknown" values are treated as unavailable.
work_arrangement_usable = (
    raw_df["REMOTE_TYPE_NAME"].notna()
    & raw_df["REMOTE_TYPE_NAME"]
        .astype(str)
        .str.strip()
        .str.lower()
        .ne("unknown")
).sum()

coverage_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "Attribute": [
        "Job Title",
        "Employer",
        "Location",
        "Observed Salary Range",
        "Minimum Experience",
        "Work Arrangement"
    ],
    "Postings with Usable Data": [
        raw_df["TITLE_CLEAN"].notna().sum(),
        raw_df["COMPANY_CLEAN"].notna().sum(),
        raw_df["LOCATION"].notna().sum(),
        raw_df[["SALARY_FROM", "SALARY_TO"]]
            .notna()
            .all(axis=1)
            .sum(),
        raw_df["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"].notna().sum(),
        work_arrangement_usable
    ]
})

coverage_data["Coverage Percentage"] = (
    coverage_data["Postings with Usable Data"]
    / total_postings
    * 100
).round(1)

coverage_data = coverage_data.sort_values(
    "Postings with Usable Data",
    ascending=True
)

# print(coverage_data)

fig_coverage = px.bar(
    coverage_data,
    x="Postings with Usable Data",
    y="Attribute",
    orientation="h",
    text="Coverage Percentage",
    template="group7",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#69558E"],
    title="Coverage of Key Job-Posting Attributes"
)

fig_coverage.update_traces(
    texttemplate="%{text:.1f}%",
    textposition="outside"
)

fig_coverage.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    height=450,
    xaxis_title="Number of Postings with Usable Data",
    yaxis_title="Attribute"
)

fig_coverage.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1,
    range=[0, total_postings + 2]
)

fig_coverage.show()
```
*Figure 3: Coverage of Key Job-Posting Attributes*

Job title, employer, and location are available for all 19 postings. Experience data is less complete, with usable minimum-experience information for 9 postings. Salary and work-arrangement data are the most limited, with only 4 usable records for each.

This difference in coverage matters when reading the rest of the EDA. The title, employer, and location findings use the full sample, while the salary, experience, and remote-work results come from much smaller subsets. Those smaller sections are still useful, but they should be read with more caution.

## Salary Distribution

Salary information is incomplete in the filtered dataset. Only postings with an originally reported salary range are included in this analysis. Missing salaries that were filled during data preparation are excluded so that the results reflect observed compensation information rather than imputed values.

```{python}

import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

salary_df = raw_df.copy()

salary_df["SALARY_FROM"] = pd.to_numeric(
    salary_df["SALARY_FROM"],
    errors="coerce"
)

salary_df["SALARY_TO"] = pd.to_numeric(
    salary_df["SALARY_TO"],
    errors="coerce"
)

salary_observed = salary_df.dropna(
    subset=["SALARY_FROM", "SALARY_TO"]
).copy()

salary_observed["SALARY_MIDPOINT"] = (
    salary_observed["SALARY_FROM"] +
    salary_observed["SALARY_TO"]
) / 2

salary_observed = salary_observed.sort_values(
    "SALARY_MIDPOINT"
).reset_index(drop=True)

# Build base label using title and employer
salary_observed["BASE_LABEL"] = salary_observed.apply(
    lambda row: (
        f"{row['TITLE_CLEAN']} ({row['COMPANY_NAME']})"
        if pd.notna(row.get("COMPANY_NAME"))
        else row["TITLE_CLEAN"]
    ),
    axis=1
)

# Number repeated labels so separate postings remain visible
salary_observed["DUPLICATE_NUMBER"] = (
    salary_observed.groupby("BASE_LABEL").cumcount() + 1
)

salary_observed["DUPLICATE_TOTAL"] = (
    salary_observed.groupby("BASE_LABEL")["BASE_LABEL"].transform("count")
)

salary_observed["LABEL"] = salary_observed.apply(
    lambda row: (
        f"{row['BASE_LABEL']} - Posting {row['DUPLICATE_NUMBER']}"
        if row["DUPLICATE_TOTAL"] > 1
        else row["BASE_LABEL"]
    ),
    axis=1
)

# print(
#     f"Postings with observed salary ranges: "
#     f"{len(salary_observed)} of {len(raw_df)}"
# )

fig = go.Figure()

for _, row in salary_observed.iterrows():

    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[
                row["SALARY_FROM"],
                row["SALARY_TO"]
            ],
            y=[
                row["LABEL"],
                row["LABEL"]
            ],
            mode="lines+markers",
            line=dict(width=4),
            marker=dict(size=9),
            showlegend=False,
            hovertemplate=(
                "<b>%{y}</b><br>"
                "Salary: $%{x:,.0f}"
                "<extra></extra>"
            )
        )
    )

fig.update_layout(
    title="Observed Salary Ranges",
    xaxis_title="Annual Salary ($)",
    yaxis_title="",
    height=560,
    margin=dict(
        l=320,
        r=40,
        t=70,
        b=50
    )
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    tickprefix="$",
    tickformat="~s"
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 4: Observed Salary Ranges*

Only 4 of the 19 postings contain an observed salary range, so the salary findings should be interpreted cautiously. The available postings show variation in both the lower and upper ends of reported compensation, but the small number of observations is not sufficient to characterize salary levels across the full selected apparel and fashion analytics market. The chart therefore presents only compensation that was explicitly reported in the source postings.

## Location Patterns

Geographic information is available for most postings. A small amount of additional standardization is applied below to consolidate obvious differences in state and city labels.

```{python}

import plotly.express as px

location_df = raw_df.copy()

location_df["STATE_CLEAN"] = (
    location_df["STATE_NAME"]
    .fillna("Unknown")
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
)

location_df["CITY_CLEAN"] = (
    location_df["CITY_NAME"]
    .fillna("Unknown")
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
)

location_df["STATE_CLEAN"] = location_df[
    "STATE_CLEAN"
].replace({
    "NY": "New York",
    "Cochituate Rd": "Massachusetts"
})

location_df["CITY_CLEAN"] = location_df[
    "CITY_CLEAN"
].replace({
    "Home Office Framingham Ma 550": "Framingham"
})

state_counts = (
    location_df["STATE_CLEAN"]
    .value_counts()
    .reset_index()
)

state_counts.columns = [
    "State",
    "Number of Job Postings"
]

state_counts = state_counts.sort_values(
    "Number of Job Postings"
)

fig = px.bar(
    state_counts,
    x="Number of Job Postings",
    y="State",
    orientation="h",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#69558E"],
    title="Job Postings by State"
)

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    yaxis_title="State",
    height=450,
    margin=dict(
        l=80,
        r=30,
        t=60,
        b=40
    )
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 5: Job Postings by State*

```{python}

import plotly.express as px

state_abbrev = {
    "California": "CA",
    "Massachusetts": "MA",
    "New York": "NY",
    "Oregon": "OR",
    "Texas": "TX"
}

map_df = state_counts[
    state_counts["State"].isin(state_abbrev.keys())
].copy()

map_df["State Code"] = map_df["State"].map(state_abbrev)

fig = px.choropleth(
    map_df,
    locations="State Code",
    locationmode="USA-states",
    color="Number of Job Postings",
    scope="usa",
    color_continuous_scale=[[0, "#F1EAF2"], [1, "#69558E"]],
    hover_name="State",
    title="Geographic Concentration of Job Postings"
)

fig.update_layout(
    height=450,
    margin=dict(
        l=10,
        r=10,
        t=60,
        b=10
    )
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 6: Geographic Concentration of Job Postings*

The 19-posting sample is concentrated in a small number of states. California and Massachusetts each account for 5 postings, followed by New York with 4 and Oregon with 3. Texas contributes 1 posting, while 1 record does not contain a usable state value. This geographic concentration appears to reflect the locations of the apparel and fashion employers represented in the filtered sample rather than a geographically representative view of the broader analytics labor market.

## Experience Requirement Distribution

Experience requirements are incomplete in the source data. This analysis uses only minimum experience values that were present in the filtered dataset before missing values were filled during data preparation.

```{python}

import plotly.express as px

experience_df = raw_df.copy()

experience_df["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"] = pd.to_numeric(
    experience_df["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"],
    errors="coerce"
)

observed_experience = experience_df[
    experience_df["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"].notna()
].copy()

experience_counts = (
    observed_experience["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"]
    .value_counts()
    .sort_index()
    .reset_index()
)

experience_counts.columns = [
    "Minimum Years of Experience",
    "Number of Job Postings"
]

experience_counts["Minimum Years of Experience"] = (
    experience_counts["Minimum Years of Experience"]
    .astype(int)
    .astype(str)
)

# print(
#     f"Postings with observed minimum experience requirements: "
#     f"{len(observed_experience)} of {len(raw_df)}"
# )

fig = px.bar(
    experience_counts,
    x="Minimum Years of Experience",
    y="Number of Job Postings",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#69558E"],
    title="Observed Minimum Experience Requirements"
)

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Minimum Years of Experience",
    yaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    height=450,
    margin=dict(
        l=60,
        r=30,
        t=60,
        b=50
    )
)

fig.update_yaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 7: Observed Minimum Experience Requirements*

Minimum experience information is available for 9 of the 19 postings. Among those records, 7 postings show a recorded minimum of 0 years and 2 postings show a minimum of 5 years. Because experience information is missing for more than half of the sample, these values should be interpreted as the requirements recorded in the available source data rather than as a complete representation of experience expectations across the selected market.

## Remote vs Onsite Patterns

Work-arrangement information is limited in the source data. Rather than assuming that postings with missing remote-status information are onsite roles, records without a reported work arrangement are retained as a separate "Not specified" category.

```{python}

import plotly.express as px

remote_df = raw_df.copy()

remote_df["WORK_ARRANGEMENT"] = (
    remote_df["REMOTE_TYPE_NAME"]
    .fillna("Not specified")
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
)

remote_df["WORK_ARRANGEMENT"] = (
    remote_df["WORK_ARRANGEMENT"]
    .replace({
        "": "Not specified",
        "Unknown": "Not specified"
    })
)

remote_counts = (
    remote_df["WORK_ARRANGEMENT"]
    .value_counts()
    .reset_index()
)

remote_counts.columns = [
    "Work Arrangement",
    "Number of Job Postings"
]

remote_counts = remote_counts.sort_values(
    "Number of Job Postings"
)

identified_arrangement = remote_df[
    remote_df["WORK_ARRANGEMENT"].isin(
        ["Hybrid", "Remote", "Onsite"]
    )
].shape[0]

# print(
#     f"Postings with an identifiable work arrangement: "
#     f"{identified_arrangement} of {len(raw_df)}"
# )

fig = px.bar(
    remote_counts,
    x="Number of Job Postings",
    y="Work Arrangement",
    orientation="h",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#69558E"],
    title="Reported Work Arrangement"
)

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    yaxis_title="Work Arrangement",
    height=420,
    margin=dict(
        l=100,
        r=30,
        t=60,
        b=40
    )
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 8: Reported Work Arrangement*

An identifiable work arrangement is available for only 4 of the 19 postings. Three postings are classified as hybrid and one as fully remote. The remaining 15 postings either do not report a work arrangement or contain an unknown value. No posting in the available sample is explicitly classified as onsite. Because work-arrangement information is unavailable for most of the sample, these results should not be used to infer the overall prevalence of remote, hybrid, or onsite work in the selected market.

## Top Employers

Employer names are standardized below to consolidate obvious duplicate labels before comparing hiring activity within the selected market.

```{python}

})

employer_counts = (

    .reset_index()
)

employer_counts.columns = [
    "Employer",

]

employer_counts = employer_counts.sort_values(

# print(

        b=40
    )

fig.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig.show()
```
*Figure 9: Top Employers in the Selected Market*

Hiring activity in the selected sample is concentrated among a small number of apparel and retail employers. Vuori and TJX each account for 5 postings, followed by Adidas with 3 and Ralph Lauren with 2. Nordstrom, Foot Locker, Michaels, and Macy’s each contribute 1 posting. These counts should be interpreted within the context of the small, intentionally filtered dataset rather than as a ranking of overall hiring activity across the apparel and fashion industry.

## Baseline Summary

The market baseline provides a descriptive snapshot of analytics-related opportunities within the selected apparel and fashion industry scope. The final dataset contains 19 verified job postings and shows that analytics work appears across several functional areas, including business intelligence, merchandising, ecommerce, finance, operations, and marketing.

Hiring activity is concentrated among a small group of employers and locations. Vuori and TJX each account for 5 postings, while California and Massachusetts each account for 5 postings. New York and Oregon also represent notable hiring locations within the sample.

Several variables have substantial missing information. Only 4 postings contain observed salary ranges, 9 contain recorded minimum experience requirements, and 4 contain an identifiable work arrangement. These limitations are retained explicitly in the analysis rather than treating imputed or missing values as if they were directly reported by employers.

Overall, the findings should be interpreted as a baseline for this narrowly defined apparel and fashion analytics market rather than as estimates of the broader analytics labor market. The results provide a foundation for the later skill-gap and career-evaluation stages of the project.
